segments.text: September 1944. Morning fog rolls over the fields of Lorraine, so thick a man cannot see ten yards. Out of that white wall come the Panthers — the finest tanks Germany has left.
segments.image_title: 39th Infantry Brigade of the US Army crossing the Siegfried Line, Germany - September 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text: Waiting in the mist are American Shermans. Smaller. Thinner-skinned. Outgunned. Every tanker in France knows the brutal math: a Panther can kill a Sherman at a mile. A Sherman has to get close enough to touch one.
segments.image_title: SC 192042 - U.S. tanks pass through the wrecked streets of Coutances, France, on their way to the sea beyond the town. 30 July, 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
This is Arracourt. And over the next twelve days, Sherman crews will learn — first the hard way, then the smart way — exactly how to fight Panthers and win.

Three weeks earlier, Patton's Third Army had torn across France so fast it outran its own fuel trucks.
segments.image_title: SC 192133 - Cavalrymen of an armored unit moving their first machine gun scout squad across the swamp to an island held by stubborn German paratroopers, near Saint-Germain on the Periers, France, front
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
Now it sat straddling the Moselle River, engines idling, waiting for gasoline. The Germans saw their chance.

Hitler ordered a counterstroke: the Fifth Panzer Army, under General Hasso von Manteuffel, would smash into the exposed American flank near the village of Arracourt and cut Patton's spearheads off at the root.
segments.image_title: SC 195550 - Members of an American tank unit ford the National Canal, near Bayon, France, as they follow the Germans retreating back towards the German frontier. 12 September, 1944. (52597565301)
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

people.license_note: Commons: Public domain / U.S. Army Signal Corps

segments.text: Manteuffel's spearhead was brand new: the 111th and 113th Panzer Brigades, built around the Panther. Long 75-millimeter gun, thick sloped armor, lethal at two thousand yards. On paper, no Sherman alive could stand in front of one.
segments.image_title: BALATON Panther LAH
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text: In the American line sat the 4th Armored Division — Major General John Wood's division, the spearhead of Patton's army. Its tankers had fought across France all summer. They were veterans.
segments.image_title: SC 192134 - Cavalrymen of an armored unit moving their first machine gun scout squad across the swamp to an island held by stubborn German paratroopers, near Saint-Germain on the Periers, France, front
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

people.image_title: File:SC 190589 - Portrait of Major General John S. Wood, 1944. (49631234753).jpg
people.license_note: Commons: Public domain / U.S. Army Signal Corps

segments.text:
But they had never met Panthers in this number.

The Panther's gun could punch through a Sherman's front plate at ranges where the Sherman's own 75 could not even scratch the Panther's glacis.
segments.image_title: SC 192120 - Vehicles of an armored unit move through the streets of Periers, France, up to the front lines. 29 July, 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
Head-on, at distance, the Sherman simply lost. Every crew knew it. The fear had a name: Panther terror.

But the Sherman had virtues the paper stats hid. It was fast, reliable, and quick to turn its turret.
segments.image_title: A Sherman tank crew of 'C' Squadron, 13th-18th Royal Hussars rest and write letters home by the side of their vehicle, Normandy, 10 June 1944. B5425
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
Its crews were experienced. And the Americans owned two weapons the Germans could not match: artillery that answered in minutes, and fighter-bombers that owned the sky.

On September 18th, the German brigades rolled forward — straight into the fog.
segments.image_title: SC 191888-S - Photo shows German prisoners taken on the outskirts of Coutances, France, during a morning shower. 29 July, 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
The mist that blinded the Americans blinded the Germans too. And in fog, the Panther's great advantage — its long-range gun — meant nothing.

Lieutenant Colonel Creighton Abrams commanded the 37th Tank Battalion, the division's hardest-hitting unit.
segments.image_title: "Cpl. Carlton Chapman...is a machine-gunner in an M-4 tank, attached to a Motor Transport unit near Nancy, France.", 11- - NARA - 531221
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
His orders were simple: let them come close. In the fog, Shermans slipped into hull-down positions along the ridgelines and waited, engines off, listening for tracks.

On the morning of September 19th, the 113th Panzer Brigade attacked out of the mist — and drove straight into an ambush.
segments.image_title: SC 335291 - U.S. Army half-tracks used to carry mechanized infantry move down into the town of Jena, Germany, which can be seen in the background. (52235928320)
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text: Shermans opened fire at point-blank range, some at less than a hundred yards. At that distance, the 75 could punch through a Panther's thinner side armor like a can opener.
segments.image_title: SC 192096 - A patrol of American infantrymen scout through the town of Coutances, France, while it is still under German 88mm fire. 29 July, 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
The 113th lost dozens of Panthers in a single morning. Its commander was killed. The brigade that was supposed to spearhead the German offensive was wrecked before lunch.

The Germans tried again and again over the following days.
segments.image_title: Five damaged German Panzer V Panthers and two U.S. M4A3 Shermans near Guébling, Moselle, France, 25 November 1944 (111-SC-197160)
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text: But their problems ran deeper than American guns. The Panther brigades were rushed into battle with green crews who had barely trained together. Their tanks broke down constantly — final drives failing, engines overheating.
segments.image_title: SC 192109 - While it is still under German 88mm fire, a patrol of American infantrymen scout through the town of Coutances, France. 29 July, 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text: Fuel ran short. German columns stalled on the roads, sitting ducks. When the fog lifted, P-47 Thunderbolts of the XIX Tactical Air Command fell on them like hawks. American artillery, directed by observers who could see everything from the ridges, shattered every attack before it formed.
segments.image_title: SC 192112 - An American infantry patrol passes an unscarred cathedral in the midst of heavy damage in Coutances, France. 28 July, 1944
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text: And the Sherman crews were learning. They stopped meeting Panthers head-on. They used the fog and the folds of the Lorraine countryside to close the distance unseen. They fired from the flanks.
segments.image_title: German counter in northern Alsace Lorraine
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
They let the tank destroyers and the artillery do the killing at range, and finished the cripples up close.

It was combined arms — infantry, armor, artillery, and air power fighting as one machine.
segments.image_title: SC 201683 - Infantrymen of 4th Armored Division, 3rd U.S. Army, pass burning German halftrack as they advance along forest road near the Rhine River, Germany. 7 March, 1945. (53009453412)
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
The Germans attacked with tanks alone, unsupported. The Americans answered with everything at once. That was the real lesson of Arracourt.

By September 29th, it was over. The Fifth Panzer Army had lost nearly two hundred tanks.
segments.image_title: US Army 4th Armored Division organization after 15 September 1943
segments.license_note: CC BY-SA 4.0 per Wikimedia Commons - attribution required (Noclador). ShareAlike: adaptations must carry the same license.

segments.text:
The 4th Armored Division had lost about twenty-five Shermans. One of the most lopsided armored victories of the entire war — won by the supposedly inferior tank.

The Sherman never became the Panther's equal, gun for gun or armor for armor.
segments.image_title: A Sherman tank and Crusader anti-aircraft tank of the Staffordshire Yeomanry, 27th Armoured Brigade, during Operation 'Goodwood', Normandy, 18 July 1944. B7522
segments.license_note: Public domain per Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

segments.text:
It did not need to be. At Arracourt, American crews proved that tactics, training, and teamwork beat raw steel. Get close. Hit the flank. Never fight fair.

That is how Sherman crews learned to fight Panthers in the fog — and it is a lesson armor officers still study today.
